questions.text: What does the `#[test]` attribute on a function indicate?

answers.text: The function should be executed as a test during `cargo test`
The function should run only in the release profile
The function automatically becomes public
The function must return `Result`

questions.explanation: `#[test]` marks an ordinary function as a test; Cargo includes it in the test binary and runs it during `cargo test`.

questions.text: Which statements about assertions in tests are true? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: `assert!(condition)` expects `true`
`assert_ne!(a, b)` checks that the values differ
`assert_eq!` and `assert_ne!` can display the compared values on failure
`assert!` automatically checks every branch of a `match`

questions.explanation: `assert!` checks a Boolean condition, while `assert_eq!` and `assert_ne!` test equality and inequality. Exhaustiveness of `match` is checked by the compiler, not by `assert!`.

questions.text: Which statements about `#[should_panic]` are true? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: The test passes if `panic!` actually occurs inside it
The `expected` parameter can check for a substring in the panic message
Without `expected`, a test can pass because of a panic for an unexpected reason
The attribute turns any compilation error into a successful test

questions.explanation: `#[should_panic]` is for expected panics. `expected` makes the check more precise by requiring a matching substring in the panic message; compilation errors are not converted into passing tests.
